blog.title: Shopify Flow vs Mechanic: Which Automation Tool Should Your Store Use?
blog.excerpt: Both tools automate your store, but they shine at different jobs. Here's how to pick the right one, or use both.
blog.body_html:
Every growing Shopify store hits the same problem: too many small manual jobs. Tagging orders, alerting the team when stock is low, sending a follow-up to a customer. Two tools solve most of this: Shopify Flow and Mechanic. I use both on client stores, and they are good at different things.

Shopify Flow in one minute

Flow is Shopify's own automation app. You build workflows visually with three pieces:

  • Trigger: something happens, like an order is created
  • Condition: check something, like the order total is over $200
  • Action: do something, like add a VIP tag to the customer

Flow is a free Shopify app, it comes with many ready-made templates, and you don't need to write code. For simple rules it is the fastest way to get started.

Mechanic in one minute

Mechanic is a third-party app from the Shopify App Store. Instead of drag and drop, each automation is a task written in Liquid, the same language Shopify themes use. It also has a large library of ready-made tasks you can install and adjust.

Because you write real logic, Mechanic can handle things Flow struggles with: loops over many products, scheduled jobs, bulk updates, building and emailing reports, or calling outside APIs. Mechanic is a paid app, so check its current pricing on the App Store.

When to use Shopify Flow

  • You want a quick rule like "tag high-value orders" or "notify me when inventory drops below 5".
  • Nobody on the team writes code and you want to edit the automation yourself.
  • A Flow template already does 90% of what you need.

When to use Mechanic

  • The logic has many steps, loops or calculations.
  • You need something to run on a schedule, like a daily stock report at 8 AM.
  • You want to update hundreds of products or orders at once.
  • You need an automation Flow simply does not offer.

Can you use both?

Yes, and many stores do. A setup I often build: Flow handles the simple everyday rules the store owner can edit, and Mechanic handles the heavy jobs like scheduled reports, fulfillment logic and bulk cleanups. This keeps the simple stuff easy to change and the complex stuff reliable.

A simple way to decide

  1. Write down the job in one sentence, for example "every Monday email me products with fewer than 3 in stock".
  2. Search the Flow templates. If one fits, use Flow.
  3. If the job needs a schedule, a loop or a report, use Mechanic.
  4. If you're unsure, start with Flow. You can move a workflow to Mechanic later when it grows.

Want your store's repetitive work automated? Tell me what you do by hand every week and I'll suggest the simplest way to automate it.

blog.title: 5 Business Tasks You Can Hand Over to a Python Bot
blog.excerpt: Price checks, alerts, daily reports and more. Five repetitive jobs a small Python bot can do for you, with a simple example.
blog.body_html:
If someone on your team opens the same websites every morning, copies numbers into a spreadsheet or checks a dashboard twenty times a day, that job can probably be done by a small Python bot. Bots don't get tired, don't forget, and run at 3 AM without complaining.

Here are five tasks I see businesses automate most often, and what each one looks like in practice.

1. Price and stock monitoring

A bot can check competitor prices, supplier stock or marketplace listings on a schedule and tell you only when something changes. Instead of checking 50 pages by hand, you get one message: "3 prices changed today".

2. Market and data alerts

Many APIs give you live data: crypto markets, exchange rates, weather, shipping status. A bot can watch these numbers and alert you when they cross a level you care about. You decide the rules, the bot does the watching.

3. Daily and weekly reports

A bot can pull numbers from Shopify, Google Sheets or any API, put them together and send a clean summary to your email or Telegram every morning. No more logging into five dashboards.

4. Moving data between tools

New order in one system needs to appear in another? A form submission needs to become a row in a sheet and a message to your team? This kind of "glue" work is perfect for automation through APIs.

5. Repetitive website tasks

Downloading invoices, checking that pages are online, collecting public information you're allowed to use. A bot can do these the same way every time and keep a log of what it did.

What a simple bot looks like

Here is a stripped-down example of a price watcher. A real one adds error handling, logging and a proper notification channel, but the idea is the same:

import requests, time

URL = "https://example.com/api/price"   # the data you want to watch
CHECK_EVERY = 15 * 60                    # seconds
last_price = None

def notify(text):
    # send to Telegram, email, Slack... here we just print
    print(text)

while True:
    price = requests.get(URL, timeout=20).json()["price"]
    if last_price is not None and price != last_price:
        change = (price - last_price) / last_price * 100
        notify(f"Price changed: {last_price} -> {price} ({change:+.1f}%)")
    last_price = price
    time.sleep(CHECK_EVERY)

Before you build a bot

  • Use official APIs when they exist. They are faster and more reliable than scraping web pages.
  • Respect the rules of the websites and platforms you connect to. Read their terms and rate limits.
  • Plan for failures. Internet drops and APIs change, so a good bot retries and tells you when something breaks.
  • Start small. Automate one painful task first, then add more.

Have a task you repeat every day? Describe it to me and I'll tell you honestly whether a bot can do it and how long it would take to build.

blog.title: How to Build a Custom Shopify Section with Liquid (Step by Step)
blog.excerpt: Build a fully editable testimonial section from scratch with Liquid, schema settings, blocks and section-scoped CSS.
blog.body_html:
Most Shopify themes come with good sections, but sooner or later a store needs something the theme does not have. Many store owners install another app for every small layout. A better option is a custom section written in Liquid. It loads faster, has no monthly fee, and the store owner can still edit everything from the theme editor.

In this guide I'll build a simple testimonial strip section from scratch. The same pattern works for almost any section you need: feature lists, logo walls, FAQs or booking blocks.

What a Shopify section is made of

A section is one .liquid file inside the sections folder of your theme. It has three parts:

  • HTML and Liquid that output the content
  • CSS that styles it
  • A schema in JSON that tells the theme editor which settings and blocks to show

Settings are for things that appear once (like a heading). Blocks are for things the merchant can add, remove and reorder (like each testimonial).

Step 1: Create the file

In your Shopify admin go to Online Store → Themes → … → Edit code. Under sections, click Add a new section and name it testimonial-strip. Always work on a duplicate of your live theme so you never break the real store.

Step 2: Write the markup

This loops through every block the merchant adds and prints the quote and the customer name:

<section class="ts-{{ section.id }}">
  <div class="ts-wrap">
    {%- if section.settings.heading != blank -%}
      <h2>{{ section.settings.heading | escape }}</h2>
    {%- endif -%}
    <div class="ts-grid">
      {%- for block in section.blocks -%}
        <figure class="ts-card" {{ block.shopify_attributes }}>
          <blockquote>{{ block.settings.quote }}</blockquote>
          <figcaption>{{ block.settings.author | escape }}</figcaption>
        </figure>
      {%- endfor -%}
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

Two details matter here. section.id gives each copy of the section a unique class, so two strips on the same page never fight over styles. And block.shopify_attributes lets the theme editor highlight the right block when the merchant clicks on it.

Step 3: Add the schema

The schema goes at the bottom of the same file. This is what makes the section editable without code:

{% schema %}
{
  "name": "Testimonial strip",
  "settings": [
    { "type": "text", "id": "heading", "label": "Heading", "default": "What customers say" },
    { "type": "range", "id": "columns", "label": "Cards per row", "min": 1, "max": 4, "step": 1, "default": 3 }
  ],
  "blocks": [
    {
      "type": "testimonial",
      "name": "Testimonial",
      "settings": [
        { "type": "richtext", "id": "quote", "label": "Quote", "default": "<p>Great product, fast shipping!</p>" },
        { "type": "text", "id": "author", "label": "Customer name", "default": "Happy customer" }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "presets": [
    { "name": "Testimonial strip", "blocks": [{ "type": "testimonial" }, { "type": "testimonial" }] }
  ]
}
{% endschema %}

The presets part is important. Without it, the section will not appear in the Add section list of the theme editor.

Step 4: Style it

Put the CSS inside a {%- style -%} tag so you can use Liquid values like the number of columns:

{%- style -%}
  .ts-{{ section.id }} .ts-wrap { max-width: 1200px; margin: 0 auto; padding: 60px 20px; }
  .ts-{{ section.id }} h2 { text-align: center; margin-bottom: 32px; }
  .ts-{{ section.id }} .ts-grid {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: repeat({{ section.settings.columns }}, minmax(0, 1fr));
    gap: 20px;
  }
  .ts-{{ section.id }} .ts-card { border: 1px solid rgba(0,0,0,.1); border-radius: 12px; padding: 24px; margin: 0; }
  @media (max-width: 749px) {
    .ts-{{ section.id }} .ts-grid { grid-template-columns: 1fr; }
  }
{%- endstyle -%}

Step 5: Add it from the theme editor

Save the file, open Customize, click Add section and choose Testimonial strip. You can now change the heading, add more testimonials and drag them into any order.

Tips that save time later

  • Use | escape on plain text settings so special characters never break your HTML.
  • Give every setting a sensible default, so the section looks good the moment it is added.
  • Keep class names prefixed with the section id to avoid clashes with the theme.
  • Test on mobile in the theme editor before you publish.

A good custom section feels like it was always part of the theme. The merchant should never need to call a developer to change a word.
